lessons.title: Testing Soil pH and Nutrient Levels
lessons.body:
Before you plant tomatoes, you need to know your soil's pH and nutrient levels. Tomatoes grow best in soil with a pH between 6.0 and 6.8. If pH is too low (acidic) or too high (alkaline), nutrients get locked up and plants can't absorb them. You can test pH with a simple DIY kit from an agro-vet shop or use a digital pH meter. For a cheap test, mix soil with distilled water (1:1) and dip a pH strip. For accurate results, send a sample to a local agricultural extension office. They often charge a small fee but give detailed nutrient reports.

To test nutrients, look for signs: yellowing leaves mean nitrogen deficiency; purple leaves suggest phosphorus deficiency; brown leaf edges indicate potassium deficiency. But visual signs appear late. Better to use a soil test kit that measures nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K). In many African countries, you can buy NPK test kits from companies like Soil Test or local agro-dealers. Follow instructions carefully: take soil from 10-15 spots in your field, mix them in a bucket, and take a cupful for testing. Test before each planting season because nutrients change with crops and rains.

If pH is below 6.0, add agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) at 2-4 kg per 10 square meters, mix into top 15 cm, and water. Wait 2-4 weeks before planting. If pH is above 7.0, add elemental sulfur or organic matter like compost or manure. For nutrients, if nitrogen is low, add manure or urea; if phosphorus is low, add rock phosphate or bone meal; if potassium is low, add wood ash or potassium sulfate. Always test first to avoid wasting money on unnecessary fertilizers. Remember, healthy soil is the foundation of a good tomato harvest.

lessons.title: Amending Soil with Organic Matter
lessons.body:
Organic matter is the life of your soil. It improves water holding, drainage, and feeds beneficial microbes. For tomatoes, aim for soil with 3-5% organic matter. Common sources in Africa include cattle manure, goat manure, poultry litter, compost, and crop residues. Never use fresh manureâit burns roots and carries diseases. Compost it first: pile manure with dry leaves, grass, and kitchen scraps, keep it moist, and turn every two weeks. In 6-8 weeks, it becomes dark, crumbly compost.

Apply compost or well-rotted manure at 2-4 kg per square meter (about 2-4 large buckets per 10 square meters). Spread it evenly over the bed and mix into the top 15-20 cm of soil with a hoe or fork. If you have limited manure, concentrate it in planting holes: mix one part compost with two parts soil. For liquid fertilizer, soak manure in water for 3 days (1 part manure to 5 parts water), strain, and use to water plants every two weeks.

In dry areas, organic matter helps soil hold water. In heavy clay, it improves drainage. You can also grow green manures like cowpeas or lablab before tomatoes, then plow them in. In sandy soils, add compost plus clay to improve structure. Avoid using sawdust unless composted, as it ties up nitrogen. Also, don't over-apply manureâtoo much causes leafy plants with few fruits. A good rule: if soil is poor, apply 4 kg per square meter; if already fertile, 1-2 kg. Always mix into soil, not just on top. Mulching with dry grass after planting also adds organic matter as it breaks down and conserves moisture.

lessons.title: Choosing Between Raised Beds, Containers, and Field Planting
lessons.body:
Your choice of planting method depends on your land, water, and soil. Raised beds are best for poor drainage, heavy clay, or small gardens. Build beds 20-30 cm high and 1 meter wide, with paths 30-50 cm between. This improves drainage, warms soil earlier, and makes weeding easier. In flood-prone areas, raised beds save your crop. Use a fork to loosen soil, then shape beds with a hoe. Add compost and mix well. Raised beds dry out faster, so mulch heavily and water regularly.

Containers work for urban growers or those with very poor soil. Use buckets, sacks, or old tiresâat least 20 liters per plant. Drill holes for drainage. Fill with a mix of 1 part compost, 1 part sand, and 1 part topsoil. Containers heat up fast; in hot climates, paint them white or shade them. Water daily. Containers are portable and allow you to control soil exactly, but they need more frequent fertilizing because nutrients leach out.

Field planting is cheapest for large areas with good soil. Plow or dig to 30 cm deep, remove rocks and roots, and level. Plant in rows 60-90 cm apart, with 45-60 cm between plants. Field planting exposes plants to more pests and diseases, so rotate crops and use mulch. If your field has hardpan, break it with a fork or chisel plow. In dry regions, sunken beds (zai pits) capture water. Choose based on your resources: raised beds for wet areas, containers for small spaces, fields for scale. Many farmers combine methodsâgrow seedlings in containers, then transplant to raised beds or fields.

lessons.title: Tilling and Bed Formation Techniques
lessons.body:
Tilling loosens soil so roots can grow. But don't over-tillâit destroys soil structure and organic matter. For tomatoes, till to a depth of 20-30 cm. Use a hoe, fork, or tractor plow. In small gardens, double-dig: remove top 30 cm of soil, loosen the next 30 cm with a fork, then replace topsoil. This is hard work but gives excellent root depth. In large fields, plow once, then harrow to break clods. Do this when soil is moist but not wetâif it sticks to your tools, wait.

After tilling, form beds. Raised beds are 1 meter wide and 20-30 cm high. Mark lines with string, then pull soil from paths onto beds using a hoe. Pat the sides firm. For flat beds, just level the soil and create shallow furrows for planting. In dry areas, make sunken beds (30 cm deep, 1 meter wide) to catch rainwater. In very wet areas, make beds 40 cm high. Add compost and mix into the top 15 cm before shaping. Beds should run east-west to maximize sunlight, or along contours on slopes to reduce erosion.

Bed formation should be done 1-2 weeks before planting. This allows soil to settle and any added amendments to integrate. If you have a tractor, use a bedder. For hand tools, a hoe and rake are enough. After forming beds, cover with mulch (dry grass, straw) to conserve moisture and suppress weeds. If you're in a windy area, make beds slightly lower and plant windbreaks like maize. Remember, good bed preparation means better drainage, easier watering, and healthier roots. Don't plant tomatoes in waterlogged soilâthey will die from root rot. Test drainage by pouring a bucket of water; if it drains within an hour, it's good.

lessons.title: Applying Base Fertilizers and Compost
lessons.body:
Base fertilizers are applied before planting to give tomatoes a strong start. The main nutrients are nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K). A common recommendation is NPK 10-10-10 or 15-15-15. Apply 200-300 grams per square meter (about 2-3 handfuls) broadcast over the bed, then mix into the top 15 cm. If using single fertilizers, apply 100g of urea (for N), 150g of triple superphosphate (for P), and 100g of muriate of potash (for K) per 10 square meters. But always test soil firstâtoo much fertilizer burns roots and wastes money.

Compost is your best base. Apply 2-4 kg per square meter, mixing it into the soil. If you have manure, use well-rotted manure at 2-3 kg per square meter. For planting holes, mix a handful of compost and a tablespoon of wood ash (for potassium) with soil. Avoid putting fertilizer directly on rootsâplace it 5-10 cm away from the stem. In sandy soils, split applications: apply half before planting, half 4 weeks later. In clay soils, one application is fine.

Timing matters: apply base fertilizers 1-2 weeks before transplanting. Water the bed after application to dissolve nutrients. If you use organic fertilizers like bone meal or fish emulsion, apply according to package instructions. For a cheap homemade mix, combine 1 part compost, 1 part crushed charcoal, and 1 part wood ash. This provides potassium and improves soil. Remember, tomatoes are heavy feeders. After the first fruits set, side-dress with nitrogen (e.g., 50g urea per plant) to support fruit development. But don't overdo nitrogenâit causes leafy plants with few tomatoes. Balanced feeding is key.

lessons.title: Soil Solarization for Disease Prevention
lessons.body:
Soil solarization uses the sun's heat to kill soil-borne diseases, nematodes, and weed seeds. It works best in hot, sunny climates with at least 6 weeks of intense sun. First, prepare the soil: till it, remove rocks and roots, and level it. Water the soil deeplyâmoist soil conducts heat better. Then cover the bed with clear plastic sheeting (UV-stabilized, 25-50 microns thick). Bury the edges in soil to trap heat. The plastic acts like a greenhouse, raising soil temperature to 50-60Â°C in the top 30 cm, which kills many pathogens.

For best results, solarize during the hottest part of the year, when temperatures are above 30Â°C. Leave the plastic on for 4-6 weeks. In cooler areas, it may take 8 weeks. After removing the plastic, avoid re-contaminating the soil: don't walk on it with dirty boots, and don't mix in fresh manure. Solarization also increases available nutrients like nitrogen and potassium. It's especially useful if you've had problems with bacterial wilt, fusarium wilt, or root-knot nematodes. These diseases can wipe out your tomatoes. Solarization is cheaper than chemicals and safe for organic farming.

However, solarization kills both harmful and beneficial microbes. After solarizing, reintroduce beneficial life by adding compost or compost tea. Also, solarization only works in the top 30 cmâdeep-rooted pathogens may survive. Combine with crop rotation: after solarizing, plant tomatoes, then rotate with maize or beans for 2-3 years. In small gardens, you can solarize individual planting holes by covering them with plastic for 2 weeks. Always use clear plastic, not blackâblack plastic absorbs heat but doesn't transmit it as well. If plastic is expensive, use it for high-value crops like tomatoes. After solarization, your soil is like a clean slateâready for healthy tomato roots.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Soil Preparation and Fertility Management for Tomato Farming

Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is one of Africa's highest-value horticultural crops, but it is also one of the most unforgiving when soil conditions are wrong. A tomato plant puts 60â80% of its energy into fruit production only when its root zone is loose, well-drained, correctly acidic, and biologically alive. In African smallholder and commercial contexts â from the Rift Valley highlands to the Guinea savanna and the Mediterranean climate of the Cape â soil preparation is not a "land preparation" chore. It is a capital investment that determines yield, disease pressure, and marketable grade. This practical reference condenses the six core lessons of this module into decision-ready guidance for farm managers and extension officers.

1. Testing Soil pH and Nutrient Levels

Tomato performs best between pH 6.0 and 6.8. Below 5.5, phosphorus locks up and aluminium becomes toxic; above 7.5, iron, manganese, zinc, and boron become unavailable, and bacterial wilt pressure rises. In much of Africa, soils are either strongly acidic (humid highlands, e.g., Kenya's Central Highlands, Rwanda, Cameroon) or alkaline (Sahel, northern Nigeria, Senegal). A laboratory test is ideal, but a portable pH meter or colour kit plus a soil auger gives actionable data at low cost. Sample 15â20 cores per hectare at 0â20 cm depth in a "W" pattern, mix in a clean bucket, and air-dry before testing.

Table 1: Soil pH interpretation and amendment rates for tomato
pH range Status Recommended amendment Rate per hectare
< 5.0Strongly acidicAgricultural lime (CaCOâ)3â5 t
5.0â5.5AcidicAgricultural lime1.5â3 t
5.6â6.0Slightly acidicWood ash or dolomitic lime0.5â1.5 t

6.9â7.5NeutralElemental sulphur (if >7.2)100â300 kg
> 7.5AlkalineElemental sulphur + gypsum300â600 kg

Sources: FAO (2021) Soil testing and plant analysis; AGRA (2019) Soil Health and Fertility in Africa; KALRO soil fertility recommendations (Kenya).

2. Amending Soil with Organic Matter

Organic matter is the single highest-return soil investment for African tomato growers. It buffers pH, holds water (critical under erratic rainfall), feeds soil biology, and suppresses soil-borne pathogens. Target 3â5% organic matter. Apply 10â20 t/ha of well-decomposed cattle manure, 5â10 t/ha of poultry litter (higher N, use carefully), or 5â8 t/ha of mature compost. In peri-urban systems, vermicompost at 3â5 t/ha is excellent but pricier. Never apply fresh manure â it burns roots and introduces E. coli and weed seeds.

Table 2: Common organic amendments â nutrient content and application guidance
Amendment N-P-K (approx.) Rate (t/ha) Best use Caution
Cattle manure (composted)0.5-0.3-0.510â20Basal dressing, all soilsWeed seeds if not composted
Poultry litter2.5-1.5-1.55â10High-N soils, quick boostSalinity, burns if fresh

Sources: FAO (2015) World fertilizer trends and outlook; CIMMYT (2018) Conservation agriculture and soil fertility; AGRA (2019).

3. Choosing Between Raised Beds, Containers, and Field Planting

Raised beds (20â30 cm high, 60â100 cm wide) are the default for humid, high-rainfall zones and for soils with poor drainage or nematode pressure. They warm earlier, improve aeration, and reduce root-zone waterlogging â the leading cause of bacterial wilt in African tomato fields. Containers (15â25 L bags, buckets, or grow-bags) suit urban and peri-urban farms, rooftop production in Nairobi, Lagos, and Accra, and controlled-environment tunnels. Field planting on flat or ridge-tilled land is cheapest per hectare and best for mechanised, large-scale production in savanna zones with deep, well-drained loams. Business rule: choose the system that matches your market. Fresh-market tomatoes for urban supermarkets reward raised beds and containers (cleaner fruit, less disease); processing tomatoes for industrial buyers reward field planting (lower cost per tonne).

4. Tilling and Bed Formation Techniques

Deep tillage to 30â40 cm breaks hardpans and lets tomato roots reach moisture. In conservation-agriculture systems, minimum tillage with ripping lines is preferred to protect soil structure and organic matter. Form beds with a tractor-mounted bedder, a two-wheel tractor, or hand hoes. Standard dimensions: bed height 20â30 cm, width 60â100 cm, path 40â50 cm. Add a 2â3 cm layer of mulch (rice straw, maize stover, or black plastic) immediately after bed formation to conserve moisture and suppress weeds. On slopes above 5%, use contour beds with cut-off drains to prevent erosion â a major yield-loss driver in Ethiopian and Rwandan highlands.

5. Applying Base Fertilizers and Compost

Base fertilizer goes into the bed at planting, not on the surface. A common African recommendation is DAP 18-46-0 at 200â250 kg/ha or NPK 17-17-17 at 300â400 kg/ha, blended with 10â20 t/ha of compost. Place fertilizer 5â8 cm below and 5 cm to the side of the seedling to avoid root burn. Top-dress with CAN or urea at 3 and 6 weeks after transplanting. For organic-only production, use poultry litter or vermicompost plus rock phosphate and wood ash. Always calibrate with a soil test â blanket fertilizer recommendations waste money and acidify soils.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Chemical and Biological Hazards

Agricultural lime, elemental sulphur, and fertilizers are corrosive or irritating. Wear gloves, eye protection, and a dust mask when handling. Never apply lime and ammonium-based fertilizer together â ammonia gas is released and can burn seedlings. Fresh manure carries E. coli, Salmonella, and parasitic eggs; compost it at 55â65 Â°C for at least 15 days before use, and wash hands and tools after handling. Store all chemicals away from children, livestock, and water sources, and follow national pesticide and fertilizer regulations (e.g., KEPHIS in Kenya, NAFDAC in Nigeria).

6. Soil Solarization for Disease Prevention

Soil solarization uses clear polyethylene mulch (25â50 Âµm) to trap solar heat and raise topsoil temperature to 45â60 Â°C for 4â6 weeks. It kills Fusarium, Verticillium, Ralstonia solanacearum (bacterial wilt), nematodes, and weed seeds in the top 20 cm. Best done in the hottest, driest months â FebruaryâMarch in southern Africa, MarchâApril in East Africa, and AprilâMay in the Sahel. Moisten soil first, lay plastic tight, and seal edges. Combine with compost and biocontrol agents (Trichoderma, Bacillus subtilis) for a "bio-solarization" effect. This is a low-cost, chemical-free tool that pays for itself in reduced wilt losses, which can reach 50â100% in infested fields.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Test soil pH and NPK before every new tomato cycle â target pH 6.0â6.8.
  • â Apply 10â20 t/ha of composted manure 2â3 weeks before transplanting.
  • â Choose raised beds for humid/high-rainfall zones; containers for urban markets; field planting for mechanised scale.
  • â Till to 30â40 cm, form beds 20â30 cm high, and mulch immediately.
  • â Place DAP or NPK 5â8 cm below the seedling at transplanting; top-dress at 3 and 6 weeks.
  • â Solarize soil for 4â6 weeks in the hottest season if bacterial wilt or nematodes are present.
  • â Keep records: pH, fertilizer rates, yields, and disease incidence per plot.
  • â Wear PPE and compost manure before use â safety is a business cost, not an option.

Further Reading

  • FAO Soils Portal â Soil Management and Fertility
  • CIMMYT â Conservation Agriculture and Soil Health Resources
  • AGRA â Soil Health and Smallholder Productivity in Africa
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization Soil Guidelines
  • IITA â Integrated Soil Fertility Management for Tomato and Vegetables

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH range for tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil with pH 6.0-6.8.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for testing soil pH at home?
options: A) pH meter or test strips
quiz.explanation: pH meters or test strips give quick readings for soil acidity.

quiz.q: What does yellowing of tomato leaves often indicate?
quiz.explanation: Yellowing leaves are a classic sign of nitrogen deficiency.

quiz.q: How many spots should you sample from a field for a soil test?
quiz.explanation: Taking 10-15 samples ensures a representative mix.

quiz.q: What should you add if soil pH is below 6.0?
quiz.explanation: Lime raises pH, making soil less acidic.

quiz.q: What is a good source of organic matter for amending soil?
quiz.explanation: Composted manure is safe and adds nutrients without burning roots.

quiz.q: How long should manure be composted before use?
quiz.explanation: Composting for 6-8 weeks kills pathogens and stabilizes nutrients.

quiz.q: What is the recommended application rate of compost per square meter?
quiz.explanation: 2-4 kg per square meter provides sufficient organic matter.

quiz.q: Which green manure can be grown before tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Cowpeas fix nitrogen and add organic matter when plowed in.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of using sawdust directly in soil?
options: A) It adds too much nitrogen
quiz.explanation: Sawdust decomposes and temporarily locks up nitrogen.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of raised beds?
quiz.explanation: Raised beds improve drainage, especially in wet areas.

quiz.q: What minimum volume container is recommended per tomato plant?
quiz.explanation: 20 liters gives enough root space for a tomato plant.

quiz.q: What is a good soil mix for containers?
options: A) 1 part compost, 1 part sand, 1 part topsoil
quiz.explanation: This mix provides drainage, nutrients, and structure.

quiz.q: In field planting, what spacing is recommended between tomato rows?
quiz.explanation: 60-90 cm between rows allows air circulation and access.

quiz.q: What is double-digging?
options: B) Loosening soil to 60 cm depth
quiz.explanation: Double-digging loosens top 30 cm and next 30 cm for deep roots.

quiz.q: When should you avoid tilling soil?
options: B) When it is wet and sticky
quiz.explanation: Tilling wet soil destroys structure and creates clods.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for raised beds in wet areas?
quiz.explanation: 40 cm high beds keep roots above waterlogged soil.

quiz.q: Why should beds run east-west?
quiz.explanation: East-west orientation allows even sunlight across the bed.

quiz.q: What is a common NPK ratio for base fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: 10-10-10 is a balanced fertilizer suitable for base application.

quiz.q: How much NPK 10-10-10 should be applied per square meter?
quiz.explanation: 200-300 g per square meter provides adequate nutrients.

quiz.q: When should base fertilizers be applied?
quiz.explanation: Applying 1-2 weeks before planting allows nutrients to integrate.

quiz.q: What is a good homemade fertilizer mix?
quiz.explanation: This mix provides potassium and improves soil texture.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid placing fertilizer directly on roots?
quiz.explanation: Direct contact with concentrated fertilizer can burn plant roots.

quiz.q: What is side-dressing?
quiz.explanation: Side-dressing is applying fertilizer alongside plants during the season.

quiz.q: What is soil solarization?
options: A) Using sun to heat soil
quiz.explanation: Solarization uses clear plastic to trap solar heat and kill pathogens.

quiz.q: What type of plastic is used for solarization?
quiz.explanation: Clear plastic transmits solar radiation to heat the soil.

quiz.q: How long should soil be solarized in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: 4-6 weeks of intense sun is enough to kill many pathogens.

quiz.q: What soil temperature does solarization aim to reach?
quiz.explanation: 50-60Â°C in top 30 cm kills most soil-borne diseases.

quiz.q: What should you do after solarization?
quiz.explanation: Adding compost reintroduces beneficial microbes killed by heat.

quiz.q: Which disease can solarization help control?
quiz.explanation: Solarization reduces soil-borne bacterial wilt and nematodes.
